Cross-module check (rule for quantitative prerequisite layer): EC124/EC140 content should ground EC109's optimisation but the diagram/tangency-condition node also needs the multivariable calculus foundation (partial derivatives) genuinely used to derive MRS=price ratio, not just the Lagrangian entry point which already covers this - however the level_curves node (which teaches the slope of a level curve = MRS/MRTS interpretation) is also directly relevant and not linked.

Rule 19/breadth check: only 3 advantage points bundled in one node and only one disadvantage-side counterpart set; a real mark scheme for fiscal policy advantages typically credits more distinct points (e.g. targeting specific sectors is separate from multiplier effects; no exchange rate side effects; can address specific market failures/inequality directly). Currently only 3 points with no separate breadth - borderline but the disadvantages side has 4 points while advantages has 3, and both are single monolithic nodes rather than split by distinct justification (rule 7). Recommend splitting into separate advantage nodes.

new_nodes.label: Advantage of fiscal policy: ability to target specific sectors/groups
new_nodes.objective: Understand fiscal policy's ability to direct spending at specific sectors or groups.
essentialPoints: Government spending can be directed at specific industries, regions, or income groups in need

new_nodes.label: Advantage of fiscal policy: multiplier effect amplifies impact
new_nodes.objective: Understand how the multiplier amplifies the initial fiscal impulse.
essentialPoints: Multiplier effect means the eventual rise in output exceeds the initial government spending increase

issues.explanation: Cross-subtopic check: floating exchange rate advantage of 'automatically adjusts to correct trade imbalances' relies on the net exports/real exchange rate depreciation mechanism, which is present, but it should also depend on the balance of payments concept it is correcting - this edge is missing.

Rule 15: this node bundles two independently markable properties - allocative efficiency (P=MC) and productive efficiency (production at minimum ATC) - as one evaluation node, rather than splitting into two distinct evaluable claims each with their own essential points and potential separate exam marks.

new_nodes.label: Allocative efficiency of perfect competition (P=MC)
new_nodes.objective: Evaluate perfect competition's allocative efficiency property.
essentialPoints: Perfect competition achieves allocative efficiency because price equals marginal cost
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Perfect Competition - consumer/producer welfare

new_nodes.label: Productive efficiency of perfect competition (minimum ATC)
new_nodes.objective: Evaluate perfect competition's productive efficiency property.
essentialPoints: Long-run competitive firms produce at minimum long-run average total cost
This is distinct from allocative efficiency and reflects efficient use of resources within the firm
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Perfect Competition - consumer/producer welfare

issues.explanation: Rule 19/adv-dis breadth check: monopoly gets only one dedicated evaluation node (ec109_monopoly_welfare_loss) covering deadweight loss; a real spec would also credit monopoly's other distinguishing features (e.g. potential for economies of scale/innovation incentive, or X-inefficiency) as separate advantage/disadvantage points, and no adv/dis breakdown exists for monopoly at all versus the thorough treatment given to oligopoly models.

new_nodes.label: Potential advantages of monopoly (economies of scale, innovation incentive)
new_nodes.objective: Evaluate possible efficiency benefits monopolies can generate despite market power.
essentialPoints: Large scale may allow monopolists to exploit economies of scale unavailable to smaller competitive firms
Guaranteed profits may fund research and innovation (Schumpeterian argument)

new_nodes.label: X-inefficiency under monopoly
new_nodes.objective: Understand the concept of X-inefficiency as an additional cost of monopoly beyond allocative deadweight loss.
essentialPoints: Lack of competitive pressure may allow costs to rise above the minimum feasible level (X-inefficiency)
Distinct from allocative deadweight loss - a productive inefficiency argument
